Human decomposition

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On the slopes of Table Mountain a team of scientists are experimenting with ground breaking ‘decomposition’ research that could help the police in real life cases.

Unique Selling Point:
When the police recover skeletonised or heavily decomposed bodies, they need forensic experts to make sense of what they’ve found. One important question in such cases is: when did the person die? The answer could be found by reconstructing the circumstances from time-since-death.

In the Western Cape - the province with the highest rise in murders in 2024 - sharp force trauma, e.g. stabbing, slashing, has been identified as one of the leading causes of death. Now, in a first-of-its kind study in South Africa, a team of scientists from the University of Cape Town have provided new insights on the role scavengers like mongoose play, and the effect of sharp force trauma on the human corpse during decomposition.


Summary:
For the last seven years forensic science research at the University of Cape Town have focused on the estimation of the time-since-death and the reconstruction of the events leading up to the discovery of human remains. The purpose of the study was to provide accurate decomposition information which will contribute to the work of the Forensic Pathology Service and the South African Police.

For the purpose of the experiment, pig bodies were used as they share many similarities with humans including organs and anatomy. (In South Africa it is illegal to use donated human bodies for decomposition research). And to replicate the forensically realistic information, clothing the pig carcasses were central to the study.

The pigs were dressed in clothes to obtain forensically realistic information as clothing degrades too.The pigs and their specially tailored outfits were central to research conducted by a group of forensic scientists known as taphonomists. They study the environmental forces that drive changes to a body after death. A key aspect is estimating time-since-death, the length of time between death and a body being recovered. Ascertaining this detail can help to identify the person and reconstruct the circumstances around their death.

The pig carcasses were left to decompose in two forensically significant Cape Town habitats, Delft on the Cape Flats, and the slopes of Table Mountain - two known hot spots for murders. In the Table Mountain experiment, pig bodies were also traumatised to match the forensic similarity of stab wounds.

The study was conducted over several seasons to compare the decomposition rate. Summer-season clothing accelerated the proceeds and the carcass weight loss was directly affected by the scavenging of the Cape grey mongoose which accelerated the decomposition rate. These findings helped deepen the understanding of how soft tissue desiccates (dries out or mummifiies), which is central to improving the accuracy of time-since-death estimations and can assist in criminal investigations.

In the heat of summer, the body rapidly desiccated, with tissues losing moisture, reaching a state of mummification in under 30 days. In the coolness of winter, the process took much longer. The bodies reached a stage of advanced decomposition and lost about 20 kg of their initial weight but never lost more weight and never reached the skeleton stage.

The Cape grey mongoose was one of the key scavengers captured on the infrared camera traps placed at the decomposition site. The study revealed that the mongooses’ daily scavenging activity had a significant effect. The experiment also revealed that the mongoose target smaller, more manageable body parts from the carcass and move them undercover to eat.

It was also the first time that the scavenging habits of the Cape grey mongoose provided the answers to a live police case - rather than looking at the traditional method of measuring the temperature and decomposition rate of the human corpse - the scavenging and scattering patterns of the mongoose was key to piecing together the puzzle.

A real live example was in 2017 when a corpse without a face and fingerprints were found on the slopes of Table Mountain. The mongoose scat was analysed and fibres matching the deceased clothing was found at the scene. A ring and a watch - found in a burrow nearby where the mongoose fed on the hand and finger - provided further identification to the deceased.

This research is the first of its kind in South Africa to implement a transdisciplinary approach to understanding the role of scavengers on the rate of decomposition of clothed and traumatised bodies. It is one of the world’s first synergistic investigations of decomposition, and the first to utilse an automated data collection approach.

The story: We will capture the deployment of the next experiment scheduled for the 13th of January. The pig bodies will be dressed, traumatised and positioned in a secured site on the slopes of Table Mountain. This study will run until the end of March when the findings will be shared with us and the programme can be broadcasted.

In addition to our own visuals we have been given access to visuals of the previous experiments on the Cape Flats dune strandveld.

The story will be told through the various disciplines and their findings. We will give an example of a real live police case to demonstrate how the accumulated insights of the study could be crucial to the identification rate of the victims of unnatural deaths by accidental or criminal means.

Script:


FINAL Script: Human decomposition
Date: 29 March 2025
Duration: 12 minutes 20 seconds

UPSOUND: Good morning… big day…

UP SOUND: So, site 4, hey?

UPSOUND: So, we’ve got two teams doing clothing and measurements. One team doing trauma.

UPSOUND: 1, 2, 3…

UPSOUND: We’re gonna have to roll it a bit.

UPSOUND: All pigs will be snouts facing this way, backs facing the mountain, trotters to the city…

LINK: Erin Bates: It’s Monday the 13th of January, day one of this unusual experiment in forensic science on Table Mountain. We have exclusive access to the site with four pig bodies clothed and wounded.

DRONE MUSIC - TABLE MOUNTAIN MIST COMING OVER THE MOUNTAIN

VO1
Table Mountain National Park…..a place of beauty and a place of crime.
Here, and especially on the Cape Flats, knife violence is rife… and stabbing is often the leading cause of death.

Dr Varushka Bachan: In Cape Town we have a lot of trauma. We do find decomposed remains on the mountain very often, especially in the Summer months.

VO2
Forensic pathologist Dr Varushka Bachan is part of this diverse team, conducting ground-breaking research on decomposition in the veld… using PIGS.

DR VARUSHKA BACHAN: FORENSIC PATHOLOGIST: OBSERVATORY FORENSIC PATHOLOGY INSTITUTE - In South Africa we aren’t allowed to study human remains for decomposition.

VO3
To the east of the park are some of the most violent suburbs in the Cape – accounting for more than half of recorded murders in the Province.

Dr Varushka Bachan: A significant percentage of our homicides are stab related cases.

VO4
This research project – led by Prof Victoria Gibbon – is about improving crime scene forensics in this specific environment.

PROF. VICTORIA GIBBON: FORENSIC ANTHROPOLOGIST - UNIVERSITY OF CAPE TOWN: We want to make sure that our data is as realistic as possible for the science, so that we can use it in medical legal death investigations.

[PAUSE]

VO5
Originally destined for the dinner table, these pigs are now playing their part in advancing forensics.

Dressed in custom-made jeans and t-shirts they are placed at four different undisclosed sites on the slopes of the mountain.

Dr Calvin Mole: We have quite limited data in terms of what the effect of trauma is on the decomposition process. If there’s trauma present, does it speed up decomposition, does it attract more insects, or is there actually no role associated with the trauma…

VO6
Dr Calvin Mole is a forensic trauma specialist and entomologist, studying the insects associated with decomposition.

DR CALVIN MOLE: ENTOMOLOGIST AND TRAUMATOLOGIST: UNIVERSITY OF CAPE TOWN - So we have done some research and looked at stabbings in particular in this case and what areas of the body are commonly stabbed. And typically we’re seeing stab wounds along the chest region or in the neck region.

VO7
To simulate real-life situations as accurately as possible the carcasses are wounded or stabbed, just like the human victims who often end up in the veld.

Dr Calvin Mole: Each of the pigs are stabbed twice, once to the thorax and once to the neck region in the clavicle and we are then going to look at how that affects the rate of decomposition.

PAUSE

VO8
The Observatory Forensic Pathology Institute is one of the busiest mortuaries in the Western Cape. In 2024 a staggering 4800 bodies ended up here.

DR VICTORIA GIBBON: FORENSIC ANTHROPOLOGIST - UNIVERSITY OF CAPE TOWN - What we have to remember constantly is that there are 9 to 10 percent of people who end up in unnatural deaths in our mortuaries who are never identified. Which equates to somewhere like 10 000 people a year across the country.

VO9
Prof Gibbon works closely with the police and forensic pathology services.

As a forensic anthropologist, her job is to identify human remains from crime scenes.

Dr Victoria Gibbon: Forensic Anthropologist - I’m normally only called when they are skeletonised, decomposed, beyond the expertise of the pathologist. So in these cases I get there and there is really very little to understand who this person was.

Erin: Why is time since death so important?

Prof Victoria Gibbon: So time since death is really important because now we have this body, unidentified, we don’t know who it is, skeletonised. So it is not just about who they were but what were the circumstances that led them to come in this place.

VO10
The weather, the environment and the scavengers all play a role.

In 2014 PhD student Dr Devin Finaughty from the University of Cape Town set up the first experiment in decomposition. Using case files from the mortuary he found the Cape Flats dune strandveld to be a hotspot for crime.
[PAUSE]
He put up his cage with the pig carcass inside… and waited…

DR DEVIN FINAUGHTY: FORENSIC TAPHONOMIST: UNIVERSITY OF THE WITWATERSRAND - I arrived at my cage a couple of days after I put my cage out and I saw pieces are missing and I thought “something is eating my pig” and I saw a little tunnel that was dug under the cage.

VO11
To catch the culprit in action, Finaughty set up a camera.

Dr Devin Finaughty: And the first data came back and it was full of Cape grey mongoose.

VO12
Interestingly, the mongoose secretly carried body parts away from the carcass and would disappear under the bushes to feed undisturbed.

A discovery that proved to be invaluable in the field…

Dr Victoria Gibbon: So here I am on a real case and the hands are missing and I am looking and I can see tunneling in the fynbos. So I said to the people, let's clear back the fynbos, about 5 meters. So we pulled back and we found both hands and we found the jewellery and we also found the watch. So I think it really is a good case to see what we are doing in the field. It directly helps us in case recovery.

[UPSOUND - BIRDS]

VO13
Scavengers disappear when people are around. Keeping human interference to a minimum is important to get accurate data for a project like this. So, Finaughty developed an automated system with a team of experts to let technology do the work. It was a world first!.

UPSOUND So this is the brains of our operation. So the computer will tell, if you set a time of the day, the computer will say to the winch, turn on, and it will lift it up for ten seconds, it will hold it there, collects the weight measures that are coming off the load cell, stores then on the onboard memory and then it puts it back down.

VO13
Using the sun to power the weather system made sense.

Erin Bates: So you are looking for things like humidity, temperature, wind?

Dr Devin Finaughty: So in addition to that we’ve got air pressure, radiation and rainfall.

[UPSOUND - insects buzzing on carcass]

VO14
Nine days after the carcasses were deployed decomposition is well on its way.
Dr Mole is keeping an eye on the insect activity as it offers vital information to the forensic team.

Dr Calvin Mole: So generally speaking how it works, a pathologist would request a consultation from a forensic entomologist. We would then go and collect the insects and rear them, identify them, and do these developmental timelines for them.

Erin Bates: So how will that then help forensic investigations?

Dr Calvin Mole: So by looking at the oldest insects that are found on a decomposing body and working backwards using temperature in the area of the preceding days and the species, we can then say this body has been lying here for x amount of days. From that it helps them to generate investigative leads in terms of searching missing person databases.

Erin Bates: So bringing trauma into the experiment, how revolutionary was that?

Dr Calvin Mole: Absolutely revolutionary! There has been almost no research which has included trauma included into that equation…

Fade to black

UPSOUND: Thanks everyone for coming…..

LINK: It is day 36 of this experiment and we are about to see what remains of the pig bodies that were placed here to decompose. You can see the clothing is still intact, it’s stained but most of the flesh is gone and there are a few insects on the clothing and there is this putrid smell.

VO15
From the outset of this experiment, everyone presumed that the wounded carcasses would decompose the fastest, but surprisingly the opposite turned out to be true.

Dr Calvin Mole: So the presence of trauma, the insects are not preferentially attracted to that trauma site. They’re still going for those traditional sites like the mouth, ears, and nose and in terms of the actual decomposition process we’re actually seeing that our sites that had trauma present the decomposition is taking place slightly longer than those without trauma.

Erin Bates: So interesting. Seems completely counterintuitive but that is what the science is for, right?

Dr Calvin Mole: Yes, So it’s still early days. We need to replicate it and keep going at it to see that the findings are consistent across seasons.

UPSOUND - You can see the bone exposed over there.

Prof Victoria Gibbon: We have a lot of data now that is completely unique. With the traumatised individuals we saw an immediate bloat starting and what we saw was this bubbling of blood coming out of the trauma wounds.

VO16
During the natural process of decomposition gases build up, the body bloats… and eventually erupts… but it seems the stab wounds allow some of the gases to escape.

Prof Victoria Gibbon: The pressure is being released in these small amounts so you don’t actually get that full burst effect, which has slowed decomposition.

[PAUSE]

Dr Varushka Bachan: We are very excited because it may indeed impact the way we investigate cases in the future and we are looking forward in learning new insights about how bodies decompose in our mountains.

Prof Victoria Gibbon: In South Africa we are not just sitting behind the times internationally, we are driving the international field of research which is amazing and exciting. So I am learning a lot about how we can make a difference in the country, I think we are making a difference, it is just not as much as could be possible.

VO17
After 36 days, exposed to the elements, little remains of the four pig bodies. The data gathered here will no doubt advance forensic crime investigations – especially on the slopes of Table Mountain...


END

PROMO 1 (NO VOICE)

Dr Varushka Bachan:
We do find decomposed remains on the mountain very often, especially in the Summer months.

Prof Victoria Gibbon:
All pigs will be snouts facing this way, backs facing the mountain, trotters to the city…


PROMO 2

VO
Crime scene investigations…

Dr Varushka Bachan: A significant percentage of our homicides are stab related cases.

VO
Groundbreaking research…

It is not just about who they were but what were the circumstances that led them to come in this place.

VO
Could pig bodies help solve the forensic mysteries around human remains?


PROMO 3

VO
Four pig carcasses in a veld…

UPSOUND: So, we’ve got two teams doing clothing and measurements. One team doing trauma.

VO
A trailblazing study, redefining forensic crime investigation.

Prof Victoria Gibbon: In South Africa we are driving the international field of research.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): On the slopes of Table Mountain a team of scientists are experimenting with ground breaking ‘decomposition’ research that could help the police in real life cases.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: When the police recover skeletonised or heavily decomposed bodies, they need forensic experts to make sense of what they’ve found. One important question in such cases is: when did the person die? The answer could be found by reconstructing the circumstances from time-since-death. In the Western Cape - the province with the highest rise in murders in 2024 - sharp force trauma, e.g. stabbing, slashing, has been identified as one of the leading causes of death. Now, in a first-of-its kind study in South Africa, a team of scientists from the University of Cape Town have provided new insights on the role scavengers like mongoose play, and the effect of sharp force trauma on the human corpse during decomposition.
metadata.Summary: For the last seven years forensic science research at the University of Cape Town have focused on the estimation of the time-since-death and the reconstruction of the events leading up to the discovery of human remains. The purpose of the study was to provide accurate decomposition information which will contribute to the work of the Forensic Pathology Service and the South African Police. For the purpose of the experiment, pig bodies were used as they share many similarities with humans including organs and anatomy. (In South Africa it is illegal to use donated human bodies for decomposition research). And to replicate the forensically realistic information, clothing the pig carcasses were central to the study. The pigs were dressed in clothes to obtain forensically realistic information as clothing degrades too.The pigs and their specially tailored outfits were central to research conducted by a group of forensic scientists known as taphonomists. They study the environmental forces that drive changes to a body after death. A key aspect is estimating time-since-death, the length of time between death and a body being recovered. Ascertaining this detail can help to identify the person and reconstruct the circumstances around their death. The pig carcasses were left to decompose in two forensically significant Cape Town habitats, Delft on the Cape Flats, and the slopes of Table Mountain - two known hot spots for murders. In the Table Mountain experiment, pig bodies were also traumatised to match the forensic similarity of stab wounds. The study was conducted over several seasons to compare the decomposition rate. Summer-season clothing accelerated the proceeds and the carcass weight loss was directly affected by the scavenging of the Cape grey mongoose which accelerated the decomposition rate. These findings helped deepen the understanding of how soft tissue desiccates (dries out or mummifiies), which is central to improving the accuracy of time-since-death estimations and can assist in criminal investigations. In the heat of summer, the body rapidly desiccated, with tissues losing moisture, reaching a state of mummification in under 30 days. In the coolness of winter, the process took much longer. The bodies reached a stage of advanced decomposition and lost about 20 kg of their initial weight but never lost more weight and never reached the skeleton stage. The Cape grey mongoose was one of the key scavengers captured on the infrared camera traps placed at the decomposition site. The study revealed that the mongooses’ daily scavenging activity had a significant effect. The experiment also revealed that the mongoose target smaller, more manageable body parts from the carcass and move them undercover to eat. It was also the first time that the scavenging habits of the Cape grey mongoose provided the answers to a live police case - rather than looking at the traditional method of measuring the temperature and decomposition rate of the human corpse - the scavenging and scattering patterns of the mongoose was key to piecing together the puzzle. A real live example was in 2017 when a corpse without a face and fingerprints were found on the slopes of Table Mountain. The mongoose scat was analysed and fibres matching the deceased clothing was found at the scene. A ring and a watch - found in a burrow nearby where the mongoose fed on the hand and finger - provided further identification to the deceased. This research is the first of its kind in South Africa to implement a transdisciplinary approach to understanding the role of scavengers on the rate of decomposition of clothed and traumatised bodies. It is one of the world’s first synergistic investigations of decomposition, and the first to utilse an automated data collection approach. The story: We will capture the deployment of the next experiment scheduled for the 13th of January. The pig bodies will be dressed, traumatised and positioned in a secured site on the slopes of Table Mountain. This study will run until the end of March when the findings will be shared with us and the programme can be broadcasted. In addition to our own visuals we have been given access to visuals of the previous experiments on the Cape Flats dune strandveld. The story will be told through the various disciplines and their findings. We will give an example of a real live police case to demonstrate how the accumulated insights of the study could be crucial to the identification rate of the victims of unnatural deaths by accidental or criminal means.
